title: R&D tax credits for architecture and engineering firms
description: Architecture and engineering firms can claim the federal R&D credit under IRC Section 41 for non-routine engineering experimentation, not aesthetic design.
summary: Architecture and engineering firms in the United States can claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 for non-routine engineering experimentation—such as novel structural systems, seismic foundations, high-performance envelopes, or custom BIM algorithms—but not aesthetic design or routine code compliance. Claims must pass the Four-Part Test, avoid the funded-research exclusion, and rely on contemporaneous project-level documentation.

body.text: Architecture and engineering firms in the United States can claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 for non-routine engineering experimentation—such as novel structural systems, seismic foundations, high-performance envelopes, or custom BIM algorithms—but not aesthetic design or routine code compliance. Claims must pass the Four-Part Test, avoid the funded-research exclusion, and rely on contemporaneous project-level documentation.

Architecture and engineering (A&E) firms operating in the United States can monetize non-routine technical design and engineering experimentation through the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41), alongside complementary energy-efficiency incentives such as the IRC Section 179D commercial buildings deduction. While routine architectural aesthetics, standard building code compliance, and conventional Building Information Modeling (BIM) drafting are statutorily excluded from the credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), technical activities aimed at resolving objective engineering uncertainties—such as validating novel low-embodied-carbon structural materials, engineering custom seismic foundations, optimizing high-performance building envelopes, or developing proprietary computational design algorithms—qualify when substantiated under the statutory Four-Part Test codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) and Treasury Regulations 26 CFR § 1.41-4.

Specifically, federal appellate and U.S. Tax Court decisions—Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2024-113 (Dec. 23, 2024), and Smith, et al. v. Commissioner (T.C. order Dec. 18, 2024; post-trial memorandum decision June 2026)—demonstrate that the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and federal courts systematically disallow A&E claims that fail either the "funded research" exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) or contemporaneous project-level substantiation of the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6).

Furthermore, statutory amendments enacted in 2025 under Section 70302 of H.R. 1, Public Law 119-21 (the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act"), updated 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) to cross-reference domestic research or experimental (R&E) expenditures under IRC Section 174A, repealing mandatory 15-year amortization for post-2024 domestic R&E costs.
Strategic R&D and Technical Parameters in the Architectural Built Environment
Strategic R&D as a Competitive Differentiator in Architectural Practice

Within modern architectural and engineering practice, research and development has shifted from an academic exercise into an operational necessity for securing complex public and private commissions. Public-sector procurement increasingly weights sustainability metrics, life-cycle performance, and technical innovation criteria during tender evaluation, while private developers demand customized engineering solutions capable of resolving severe site-specific, structural, and environmental constraints. Industry commentary from architectural practice software provider OOTI confirms that applied research in an architectural practice functions as a "real competitive asset" when design agencies pair conceptual investigation with interdisciplinary engineering execution.

Through structured R&D workflows, architectural and engineering practices refine core delivery methodologies—most notably through advanced applications of Building Information Modeling (BIM) that streamline multi-disciplinary structural coordination, clash detection, and construction sequencing—while expanding into higher-margin service lines such as specialized technical consultancy, project ownership assistance, and technical mediation. This operational evolution creates a dual economic return: internal software and material research directly increases design margin by compressing rework cycles, while simultaneously generating potential tax-credit recovery if the underlying technical work satisfies federal statutory criteria.

A critical jurisdictional distinction must be maintained when evaluating industry literature on architectural R&D. Unlike European innovation regimes that often accommodate broader conceptual or aesthetic design innovation, the U.S. regime under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) imposes a strict scientific and engineering gatekeeping standard that excludes aesthetic, cosmetic, or purely architectural form-making activities.
Environmental Catalysts: Decarbonization, Embodied Carbon, and Digitalization

The technical parameters of qualifying R&D in the U.S. built environment are heavily propelled by global decarbonization mandates, stringent building energy codes, and material resource constraints. According to empirical industry data published by Saint-Gobain's Sustainable Construction Observatory, the global construction and building sector accounts for almost 40% of global carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>) emissions, consumes 50% of natural resources, and generates 40% of solid waste. Furthermore, Saint-Gobain's demographic and urban modeling projects that while 80% of the buildings that will be in use in 2050 already exist today, 50% of the total building stock expected by 2050 has yet to be constructed to accommodate an estimated global population of 9.6 billion, 70% of whom will reside in urban areas. This twin imperative—deep energy retrofitting of existing structures alongside high-efficiency new urban construction—forces A&E firms to engineer structural and mechanical solutions that depart from historical handbook specifications.

To align with the United Nations Global Compact "Business Ambition for 1.5°C" pledge and reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, leading building material manufacturers and A&E firms have established interim 2030 targets validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). As documented in Saint-Gobain North America's verified sustainability commitments (https://www.saint-gobain-northamerica.com/sustainability, updated from the legacy URL /who-we-are/innovation), these interim 2030 milestones include a 33% reduction in absolute Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions and a 16% reduction in Scope 3 emissions measured against a 2017 baseline, alongside reducing virgin raw material consumption by 30% and cutting non-valorized production waste by 80%.

For architecture and engineering firms, these macro-level environmental mandates translate into qualifying project-level R&D only when design teams must engineer, model, and empirically validate non-standard structural, geotechnical, or mechanical assemblies whose performance cannot be established from standard building codes or manufacturer tables. Verified technical innovation drivers across the A&E value chain coalesce around three interconnected engineering domains: low-carbon material integration, high-performance envelope and mechanical engineering, and custom computational design workflows.

In the domain of low-carbon material integration and structural validation, qualifying technical uncertainty arises when firms incorporate proprietary low-embodied-carbon materials into complex structural designs where standard engineering performance tables do not establish structural behavior under site-specific conditions. For example, Holcim's proprietary ECOPact low-carbon concrete utilizes supplementary cementitious materials and specialized admixture technology to deliver at least a 30% reduction in embodied CO<sub>2</sub> emissions per cubic meter compared to standard Ordinary Portland Cement (CEM I) concrete of the same compressive strength class (calculated against 2020 local industry average A1–A3 cradle-to-gate emissions without carbon offsets), with specialized formulations incorporating 10% to 100% recycled construction and demolition materials by weight via ECOCycle technology. When an A&E firm conducts systematic physical testing, finite-element modeling, or structural simulation to eliminate technical uncertainty regarding how such novel cementitious mixes perform under project-specific load paths, early-age curing thermal gradients, long-term creep, or seismic shear demands, those evaluative activities move beyond routine material specification into potentially qualifying research under IRC Section 41.

Similarly, the engineering of high-performance building envelopes and integrated mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) systems generates qualifying research when design teams develop bespoke unitized curtain walls, kinetic or double-skin facades, or specialized HVAC configurations intended to surpass baseline energy codes through iterative thermal bridging calculations, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) airflow simulations, and acoustic isolation modeling. Parallel to physical building systems, digital transformation and custom BIM workflows constitute a third major locus of A&E experimentation, encompassing the development of proprietary software plugins, parametric generative design scripts, and automated geometric or structural calculation modules within BIM environments that resolve computational bottlenecks, automate structural optimization, and reduce downstream construction rework.
Statutory Framework: Applying the IRC Section 41 Four-Part Test to A&E Activities
Statutory Mechanics of IRC Section 41(d) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4

To monetize technical innovation under federal tax law, an architecture or engineering firm must demonstrate that its technical activities satisfy the statutory definition of "qualified research" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulations 26 CFR § 1.41-4 (promulgated via T.D. 8930 and T.D. 9104 in Internal Revenue Bulletin 2004-06)—universally recognized in federal tax practice as the Four-Part Test. Because architectural practice inherently blends aesthetic spatial design with applied physical engineering, IRS examination scrutiny centers on separating subjective or cosmetic design iterations—which are explicitly excluded from the credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii)—from verifiable scientific or engineering experimentation.

Every claimed "business component"—defined under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer—must independently satisfy all four statutory prongs.
1. The Section 174 / Section 174A Expense and Elimination of Uncertainty Test

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) and (a)(3), the claimed research expenditures must be eligible to be treated as specified domestic research or experimental (R&E) expenditures under IRC Section 174A (or IRC Section 174 under prior statutory law and existing Treasury Regulations). Pursuant to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information only if it is intended to "eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component". Objective technical uncertainty exists when the information available to the taxpayer at the outset of the activity does not establish either (a) the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or (b) the appropriate design of the business component. Crucially, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), an A&E firm is not required to seek information that exceeds or expands the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the broader engineering field, nor must the experimental research ultimately succeed in practice, provided objective uncertainty existed for the taxpayer at the outset and systematic investigative activities were undertaken to resolve it.

Practitioners must account for a major 2025 legislative amendment governing this first prong. In 2025, Section 70302 of H.R. 1, Public Law 119-21 (the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act"), repealed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (P.L. 115-97) mandate that had forced taxpayers to capitalize and amortize domestic R&E expenditures over 15 years for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021. Public Law 119-21 restored immediate expensing for domestic R&E expenditures incurred after December 31, 2024 under newly codified IRC Section 174A, and simultaneously granted eligible small businesses meeting the 26 U.S.C. § 448(a)(3) gross-receipts test—defined as average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the three tax years prior to 2025—the ability to elect retroactive immediate expensing for domestic R&E expenditures incurred after December 31, 2021. While professional commentary in the AICPA's The Tax Adviser (September 30, 2025) inadvertently referred in text to "Sec. 179A" when describing the restored immediate expensing provision, the codified statutory text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) explicitly cross-references "section 174A". Because codified statutory text carries controlling legal authority over secondary commentary, tax compliance filings and legal briefs must cite 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) and IRC Section 174A.
2. The Technological in Nature Test

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), the process of experimentation utilized to discover information must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), an A&E firm does not need to invent novel scientific laws; the firm may employ existing technologies and rely on established principles of structural engineering, geotechnical mechanics, thermodynamics, acoustics, material science, or computer science to satisfy this requirement.
3. The Permitted Purpose / Business Component Test

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), the application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, relating specifically to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Pursuant to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), research does not relate to a qualified purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Consequently, architectural massing studies conducted purely for visual proportion or interior finish selections conducted for aesthetic appeal must be rigorously segregated and excluded from qualified research claims.
4. The Process of Experimentation Test and the 80% "Substantially All" Threshold

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and (a)(6), "substantially all" of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation related to a qualified purpose. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a valid process of experimentation requires a structured three-stage investigative methodology in which the taxpayer first identifies the specific technical uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the business component, next identifies one or more technical alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and finally identifies and conducts a systematic evaluative process—such as computational modeling, numerical simulation, physical prototyping, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology—to evaluate those alternatives.

Crucially, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the statutory "substantially all" requirement is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities for that business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.

If an overall building design project fails the Four-Part Test when evaluated holistically as a single business component—for instance, because routine drafting, code compliance, and construction administration consume more than 20% of total project hours—Treasury Regulations 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) provide a mandatory "shrinking-back" rule. This regulation instructs that the Four-Part Test be reapplied at the level of the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention (such as a discrete long-span structural truss subsystem, a specialized seismic foundation assembly, or a custom laboratory HVAC exhaust system) until either a qualifying subcomponent is reached that independently satisfies the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold or the most basic element of the design fails to qualify.

Resolving complex structural load paths, geotechnical/seismic foundation behavior, or high-performance facade thermal bridging where standard codes and vendor data are insufficient.
Evaluative process must fundamentally rely on principles of physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.
Relying on structural mechanics, geotechnical engineering, thermodynamics, acoustics, material science, or computational geometry rather than visual or aesthetic design.
Must aim to create a new or improve an existing function, performance, reliability, or quality of a discrete business component; excludes style, taste, or cosmetic design.
Enhancing structural durability, seismic resilience, energy efficiency, acoustic isolation, or construction assembly efficiency of a building system or software workflow.

At least 80% of research activities (by cost or reasonable basis) must involve identifying uncertainty, formulating alternatives, and systematically evaluating them via modeling, simulation, or trial-and-error.
Conducting iterative finite-element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD) airflow simulations, physical mock-up destructive testing, or custom BIM algorithm testing.

body.text: Financial Optimization: Synchronizing Section 41, Section 179D, and QRE Calculations
Strategic Synergy Between IRC Section 41 and Section 179D

Architecture and engineering firms occupy a uniquely advantageous position in the U.S. Internal Revenue Code because they can concurrently claim the IRC Section 41 R&D Tax Credit and the IRC Section 179D Energy-Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction on the same underlying construction project, provided each incentive's distinct statutory predicates are met. Rather than duplicating tax benefits for the same economic event, the two provisions reward orthogonal dimensions of sustainable building design.

IRC Section 41 operates as a process-based tax credit that provides a direct, dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal tax liability—offsetting federal income taxes for established profitable firms, or offsetting federal payroll taxes for eligible qualified small businesses (startups under five years old with less than $5 million in annual gross receipts), with unused general business credits carried back 1 year and carried forward for up to 20 years—specifically rewarding the experimental engineering process. Section 41 compensates the A&E firm for qualified employee wages, consumed prototyping supplies, third-party cloud computer leasing used for engineering simulations, and eligible third-party engineering contractor costs incurred during the iterative modeling, simulation, and testing of novel building systems.

Conversely, IRC Section 179D operates as an outcome-based tax deduction that provides an accelerated deduction based on the verified energy performance outcome of the completed building—specifically rewarding the successful design and installation of energy-efficient interior lighting systems, heating, cooling, ventilation (HVAC), and hot water systems, or building envelope systems in commercial or government buildings that surpass statutory ASHRAE energy-efficiency benchmarks.

By harmonizing both statutory incentives within internal project accounting workflows, an A&E firm lowers the effective after-tax cost of sustainable innovation twice across the project lifecycle. Section 41 cushions the upfront financial risk of engineering trial-and-error during Schematic Design and Design Development—importantly covering experimental iterations that fail to achieve performance targets and are ultimately discarded before construction—while Section 179D rewards the verified energy savings of the final deployed commercial building assembly.
Distinguishing Routine Professional Practice from Qualifying R&D

The most frequent operational error committed by A&E firms—and by generalist tax preparers—is misclassifying standard professional diligence as qualifying R&D, or, conversely, failing to isolate genuine engineering experimentation buried inside complex design phases. Both technical tax guidance and the U.S. Tax Court's December 2024 memorandum opinion in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo 2024-113) enforce a rigid boundary between linear routine design progression and the cyclical, hypothesis-driven iterative experimentation required under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5).

Specifically, executing a standard linear six-stage architectural and engineering design workflow—(1) gathering Basis of Design requirements, (2) drafting Schematic Design block diagrams, (3) coordinating Design Development plans, (4) selecting commercial equipment for Construction Documents, (5) soliciting contractor bids during Bidding, and (6) overseeing Construction Administration—does not automatically constitute a statutory process of experimentation. Activities that rely on established municipal building codes, historical reference data, standard psychrometric or load-sizing calculations, or off-the-shelf CAD/BIM software features are routine professional services excluded from Section 41. Conversely, activities requiring systematic evaluation of competing engineering alternatives to resolve objective design uncertainty satisfy the statutory criteria across the four core built-environment disciplines.

cells: Applying conventional structural engineering formulas using commercial software packages and established building codes.

Engineering novel structural systems (e.g., custom long-span trusses, diagrids, or cantilevered assemblies) requiring iterative finite-element modeling and load testing to eliminate design uncertainty.
Designing standard shallow spread footings, retaining walls, or site grading plans based on routine geotechnical soil reports.

Engineering bespoke deep-foundation piling systems or adapting construction sequencing via systematic trial-and-error to overcome complex seismic hazards, liquefaction zones, or unpredictable soil conditions.
Achieving LEED or BREEAM certification by specifying pre-approved commercial energy-efficient products, or performing basic HVAC duct-sizing calculations from known airflow tables.

Designing and validating a novel building envelope, custom MEPF configuration, or structural mix using proprietary low-CO<sub>2</sub> concrete (such as ECOPact) where structural or thermal performance requires empirical validation.
Using commercially available CAD or BIM software packages for routine 3D drawing production, quantity takeoffs, and standard clash detection.
Coding proprietary software plugins, custom parametric scripts, or automated algorithmic methodologies within BIM to optimize complex project delivery beyond existing software capabilities.

body.text: Statutory Rules for Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1), an A&E firm's total Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) equal the sum of its in-house research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2) and its contract research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3) paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on its trade or business. Each expenditure category is governed by strict statutory inclusion rules and percentage caps.

In-house employee wages under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and (B) encompass taxable wages as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a) (or self-employed earned income for partners and sole proprietors under 26 U.S.C. § 401(c)(2), explicitly excluding any wages taken into account in computing the Work Opportunity Credit under 26 U.S.C. § 51(a)) paid or incurred for "qualified services". Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), qualified services consist of engaging directly in qualified research, engaging in the direct supervision of qualified research (first-line technical supervision of experimental work, excluding higher-level executive management), or engaging in the direct support of qualified research (such as technicians fabricating physical test models or compiling simulation data). Under the statutory "substantially all" employee wage rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), if at least 80% of an employee's total services during the taxable year consist of qualified services, 100% of that employee's annual wages qualify as QREs; if an employee spends less than 80% of total annual time on qualified services, only the contemporaneously tracked percentage of wages devoted to qualified services may be included.

In-house supplies used in research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and (C) include 100% of amounts paid or incurred for tangible property consumed directly in conducting qualified research—such as physical scale-model materials, custom facade extrusion mock-ups, or low-carbon concrete test cylinders destroyed during compressive and shear testing. Critically, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C) explicitly excludes land or improvements to land, and any property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. In addition, computer use payments for research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) cover amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers directly in conducting qualified research, such as third-party high-performance cloud computing clusters leased specifically to execute intensive computational fluid dynamics (CFD) or nonlinear seismic time-history simulations.

Finally, contract research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A)–(D) are generally capped at 65 percent of amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any non-employee person (such as third-party structural specialists, acoustic engineers, or commercial wind-tunnel testing laboratories) for qualified research conducted on the taxpayer's behalf, provided the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the research, the research is performed at the taxpayer's risk, and the taxpayer retains substantial rights. While 65% is the general statutory cap under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A), the statute substitutes 75 percent for amounts paid to a tax-exempt 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) or § 501(c)(6) qualified research consortium under § 41(b)(3)(C), and 100 percent for amounts paid for qualified energy research to eligible small businesses (firms with 500 or fewer employees), universities, or federal laboratories under § 41(b)(3)(D).

cells: Direct pro-rata % of qualified services time; 100% of annual wages if qualified services ≥ 80% of total employee time.
W-2 wages or partner earned income for direct experimentation, first-line technical supervision, or direct support; excludes § 51(a) Work Opportunity Credit wages and general executive overhead.
100% of eligible non-depreciable tangible property consumed in research.
Consumed physical mock-up extrusions, scale models, and concrete test cylinders; explicitly excludes land, land improvements, and depreciable capital equipment.
100% of qualifying third-party computer use payments directly for research.
Third-party cloud computing cluster fees incurred specifically to run high-load FEA, CFD, or parametric structural simulations.
65% general cap; 75% for § 501(c)(3)/(c)(6) research consortia; 100% for eligible small business/university/federal lab energy research.
Third-party wind-tunnel testing labs, geotechnical testing specialists, or acoustic engineering subconsultants where the A&E firm bears financial risk and retains substantial rights.

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example: Calculating A&E QREs and Gross R&D Tax Credit

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) and verified credit calculation rates, consider a hypothetical structural and facade engineering firm, Meridian Built Environment Engineers, Inc., which conducts a qualifying R&D project in Tax Year 2025 to engineer a base-isolated seismic foundation and custom unitized double-skin curtain wall for an irregular high-rise site. Contemporaneous project time logs, general ledger supply accounts, and third-party laboratory contracts substantiate a five-step statutory calculation.

In the first step, Meridian computes its in-house qualified wage expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and (B). A Lead Structural Engineer earns annual W-2 wages of $150,000, and contemporaneous project time logs verify that 1,700 of her 2,000 total annual hours (85%) were spent performing iterative nonlinear seismic finite-element modeling to resolve foundation design uncertainty. Because 85% meets or exceeds the statutory 80% "substantially all" employee wage threshold under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), 100% of her annual wages qualify as QREs (Qualified Wages (Lead Engineer) = $150,000 × 100% = $150,000). Additionally, a Facade Project Architect earns annual W-2 wages of $100,000, and contemporaneous time logs verify that 600 of his 2,000 total annual hours (30%) were spent running iterative two-dimensional thermal-bridging and condensation simulations on alternative mullion profiles, while the remaining 70% was spent on routine construction document drafting and bidding coordination. Because 30% is below the 80% threshold, only the directly tracked 30% qualifies (Qualified Wages (Facade Architect) = $100,000 × 30% = $30,000), bringing Total Qualified Wages across both employees to $150,000 + $30,000 = $180,000.

In the second and third steps, Meridian computes its in-house supply expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and (C) and its contract research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A). The firm purchases $25,000 of non-depreciable custom aluminum extrusions and low-carbon concrete test cylinders that are consumed and destroyed during structural load and air-water infiltration mock-up testing; applying the 100% statutory inclusion rate yields Qualified Supplies = $25,000 × 100% = $25,000. Simultaneously, the firm pays $50,000 to an independent commercial wind-tunnel testing laboratory in the United States under a prepaid testing contract where Meridian retains substantial rights to the aerodynamic data and bears the financial risk of test failure; applying the general statutory 65% contract research cap yields Qualified Contract Research = $50,000 × 65% = $32,500.

In the fourth step, Meridian sums its in-house wages ($180,000), in-house supplies ($25,000), and contract research expenses ($32,500) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1) to establish Total QREs of $237,500. In the fifth step, Meridian applies verified gross credit calculation rates to this $237,500 QRE base. For a firm in its 4th year of claims and beyond, a statutory base amount (50% of the average QREs for the three preceding tax years under the ASC method) is subtracted from current-year QREs, and the excess QRE line is multiplied by 14%; if Meridian's statutory base amount is $112,500, its excess QREs equal $237,500 − $112,500 = $125,000, yielding Gross Credit (Year 4+) = $125,000 × 14% = $17,500.

Sum of in-house wages, supplies, and capped contract research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1))

body.text: Compliance, Documentation, and Judicial Scrutiny in the A&E Sector
Contemporaneous Documentation and the Redesigned Form 6765 Mandate

Across IRS examinations and federal litigation, the primary driver of R&D tax credit disallowance in the A&E sector is not the absence of genuine engineering innovation, but the failure to maintain contemporaneous, project-level documentation linking employee hours and costs to specific experimental tasks and discrete business components. Following federal appellate and district court litigation over refund claim specificity in United States v. Harper, 847 Fed. App'x 408 (9th Cir. 2021), and Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-cv-890 (D. Utah July 15, 2022), the IRS fundamentally restructured its upfront administrative substantiation rules.

Effective for amended return refund claims filed after January 10, 2022 (announced via IRS News Release IR-2021-203), the IRS initially mandated five essential items of factual information at the time of filing. On June 18, 2024 (via IRS FAQ 21, IRS Sets Forth Required Information for a Valid Research Credit Claim for Refund), the IRS streamlined this administrative gate by waiving two items at the time of initial refund filing—specifically the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the specific information each individual sought to discover (while explicitly reserving the right to demand both during an audit examination)—while continuing to enforce three mandatory upfront disclosures for a refund claim to be considered valid. Under this binding administrative standard, a taxpayer filing a refund claim must identify all business components to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that tax year, provide a narrative description of all research activities performed for each business component, and state the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be satisfied by properly completing Form 6765).

Simultaneously, the 2024 redesign of Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) institutionalized upfront project-level transparency on original as well as amended tax returns. As detailed in the AICPA's The Tax Adviser (October 31, 2025), the revised Form 6765 requires taxpayers to organize their quantitative and qualitative substantiation around three fundamental IRS audit inquiries: answering "What did you make?" by identifying each discrete architectural or engineering business component (or subcomponent under the shrinking-back rule) and specifying whether it is held for sale, lease, license, or internal use; answering "Why is it qualified?" by explaining the objective technical uncertainty that existed at the outset of the design phase and detailing the systematic process of experimentation (modeling, simulation, iterative testing) used to resolve it; and answering "How much did it cost?" by providing rigorous project-level time and cost accounting that segregates qualifying experimental engineering hours from routine schematic drafting, code verification, contractor bidding, and construction administration.
Landmark 2024–2026 Judicial Precedents Governing A&E Claims
Together, these three rulings establish the controlling judicial boundary for A&E R&D tax credit claims in the United States.
1. The "Funded Research" Exclusion: Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner (8th Cir. 2024)

In Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986, No. 23-1523 (8th Cir. May 6, 2024), structural engineering firm Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (MBJ) claimed approximately $190,000 in federal R&D tax credits across its fiscal years ended September 30, 2010, September 30, 2011, and September 30, 2013, for creating structural building designs for commercial, healthcare, and educational projects under fixed-price contracts. On May 6, 2024, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed the U.S. Tax Court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the IRS, disallowing 100% of the claimed credits under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) (the "funded research" exclusion) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d).

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1), research performed for another person under contract is statutorily disqualified as "funded" unless the taxpayer both (a) retains substantial rights in the research, and (b) bears the financial risk of failure, meaning that payment to the A&E firm is explicitly "contingent on the success of the research". Distinguishing the landmark defense-contracting precedent Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995)—where the contractor's payment turned on satisfying over 1,000 pages of detailed technical aircraft specifications with refundable progress payments until line-by-line technical acceptance—and aligning with Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States and United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), the Eighth Circuit held that MBJ's fixed-price contracts merely required adherence to a general professional standard of care, municipal building code compliance, and standard client review. The appellate court emphasized a critical doctrinal distinction for all A&E contracts: contractual provisions conditioning payment on the "proper performance" of professional design services do not make payment contingent on the "successful performance" of uncertain technical research.
2. Failure of the Four-Part Test and 20% Accuracy-Related Penalties: Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo 2024-113)

In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2024-113, Dkt. No. 4759-22 (U.S. Tax Court, Dec. 23, 2024), Phoenix Design Group (PDG), a C-corporation consulting engineering firm specializing in mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) systems for hospitals, universities, and commercial buildings, executed 409 engineering projects between 2013 and 2016. A third-party R&D study consultant screened the portfolio, identified 238 projects as potentially qualifying, selected a statistical sample of 24 projects, concluded that 20 of those sample projects qualified, and mathematically extrapolated those findings across all 238 projects. Based on this extrapolation, PDG claimed $562,798 in generated R&D tax credits ($138,205 in 2013; $158,031 in 2014; $138,334 in 2015; and $128,228 in 2016) and utilized $461,741 of those credits to offset federal tax liabilities across tax years 2015 through 2019 ($55,504 in 2015; $47,811 in 2016; $219,177 in 2017; $68,147 in 2018; and $71,102 in 2019).

Following a trial that examined a non-binding representative sample of three major projects—the Gerald Champion Military Psychiatric Unit, Baptist Memorial Health North Mississippi Oxford, and the Vanderbilt University Engineering and Science Building—the U.S. Tax Court disallowed 100% of the claimed R&D credits and sustained $91,806 in 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662 ($11,101 for 2015; $9,021 for 2016; $43,835 for 2017; $13,629 for 2018; and $14,220 for 2019).

The Tax Court's opinion established three foundational compliance holdings that directly govern engineering practice. First, the court held that linear design phases do not constitute iterative experimentation: PDG's standardized six-stage linear design sequence (Basis of Design, Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Document, Bidding, and Construction Administration) reflected standard engineering project management rather than a scientific process of experimentation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). Second, the court ruled that routine engineering calculations do not eliminate objective uncertainty: performing standard engineering calculations using available historical data—such as sizing HVAC ductwork from established room airflow requirements—and modifying drawings to comply with building codes or client budget changes constituted routine professional practice rather than investigative research. Third, the court confirmed that generic timesheets defeat both the 80% rule and the shrinking-back rule: because PDG's employee timesheets recorded time under broad, generic billing categories (such as "design" or "project coordination") without segregating experimental tasks from routine drafting, and because PDG's president offered retrospective oral estimates of qualifying time percentages at trial without contemporaneous corroboration, PDG could neither prove that 80% of its activities constituted a process of experimentation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) nor invoke the shrinking-back rule under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to isolate discrete MEPF subcomponents.
3. Architectural Partnership Funded Research Scrutiny: Smith, et al. v. Commissioner (2024–2026)

In Smith, et al. v. Commissioner, involving the prominent Chicago architectural partnership Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture LLP (AS+GG) and six landmark domestic and international architectural projects (including the supertall Kingdom Tower and the Masdar Headquarters complex), the IRS challenged millions of dollars in claimed R&D credits under the funded-research exclusion. On December 18, 2024, the U.S. Tax Court initially issued an order denying the IRS's motion for summary judgment on the funded-research issue because AS+GG presented contractual evidence of retained intellectual property rights and milestone-tied payment structures, sending the case to a full trial in March 2025.

However, in its subsequent post-trial memorandum decision (Smith, et al. v. Commissioner, reported in June 2026), the U.S. Tax Court ultimately disallowed the architectural partnership's R&D tax credits under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H). Applying a strict two-step funded-research analytical framework, the Tax Court focused first on whether the architecture firm retained "substantial rights" in the underlying technical research under the express terms of its client agreements, demonstrating that even world-renowned supertall and sustainable architectural designs will lose Section 41 eligibility if client contracts transfer exclusive ownership or restrict the firm's independent commercial reuse of the developed technical findings.

body.text: The Four-Step A&E Assessment Workflow and Strategic Recommendations

Synthesizing the codified requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) and (d), the 2025 legislative restoration of domestic R&E expensing under IRC Section 174A (P.L. 119-21), the upfront substantiation rules of the redesigned Form 6765, and the judicial holdings in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Phoenix Design Group, and Smith, A&E firm leadership should institutionalize a disciplined four-stage assessment and compliance workflow.
1. Contractual and Project Discovery (Pre-Design Gatekeeping)

Before commencing Schematic Design, A&E legal and tax teams must review client master services agreements (MSAs) and project contracts against the two-prong funded-research test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d). To avoid the complete credit disallowances suffered by the structural and architectural taxpayers in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson and Smith, contracts for technically uncertain projects must explicitly preserve the A&E firm's substantial rights to reuse the underlying engineering methodologies, computational scripts, and technical findings across future commissions without paying royalties or seeking client permission, while simultaneously tying fee entitlement and milestone acceptance to objective technical performance specifications (with clear financial exposure for remediation, redesign, or non-acceptance if technical parameters are not achieved) rather than generic professional standard-of-care covenants.
2. Contemporaneous Technical Uncertainty and Experimentation Logging

Project principals, structural engineers, and MEPF leads must contemporaneously document objective technical uncertainties at the outset of Schematic Design and Design Development under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3). Rather than relying on retrospective post-year-end interviews—which the U.S. Tax Court rejected in Phoenix Design Group—project teams should maintain real-time engineering logs recording why standard building codes, ASHRAE tables, geotechnical reports, or vendor specifications could not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design of the system. These contemporaneous technical records must further document the competing engineering hypotheses and design alternatives formulated to resolve that uncertainty, alongside the iterative finite-element analyses (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD) runs, thermal-bridging models, physical mock-up tests, or custom BIM scripts executed to evaluate those alternatives, retaining dated simulation outputs and failed design iterations as verifiable audit evidence.
3. Subcomponent Cost Allocation and "Shrinking-Back" Readiness

A&E firms must reconfigure internal ERP and time-tracking systems (such as Deltek Vision/Vantagepoint or OOTI) to eliminate generic billing codes like "design" or "project coordination". Time-tracking architectures must require engineers and architects to log hours against discrete building subcomponents—such as a seismic base-isolation foundation, a long-span roof truss, a custom laboratory exhaust CFD model, or an ECOPact concrete structural validation assembly—and distinguish between experimental modeling or testing tasks and routine drafting or construction administration. This granular subcomponent accounting accomplishes two critical legal objectives: it enables the firm to prove quantitatively that at least 80% of the activities within each claimed subcomponent constitute elements of a process of experimentation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), and it preserves automatic fallback eligibility under the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) if an IRS examiner challenges the holistic building design as a single business component, while simultaneously identifying employees who cross the 80% "substantially all" wage threshold of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B).
4. Audit-Ready Submission and Multi-Incentive Synchronization

Prior to filing original or amended returns, the firm—working with qualified independent R&D specialists operating under non-contingent fee structures and multi-layered technical and tax review protocols—must compile a contemporaneous Form 6765 defense file that directly answers the IRS's three core inquiries (what business component was developed, why the activity satisfies the Four-Part Test, and how QREs were computed per component). Simultaneously, tax leadership should synchronize federal IRC Section 41 filings with state-level R&D tax credits, IRC Section 174A domestic R&E expensing elections (including evaluating retroactive post-2021 immediate expensing elections for eligible firms with ≤ $31 million in average gross receipts under Public Law 119-21), and IRC Section 179D energy-efficiency commercial building deductions to maximize total after-tax recovery without double-counting expenditures.
